events.title: Accession of Claudius
events.summary: Found hiding in the palace after Caligula's murder, the 50-year-old Claudius was taken to the praetorian camp and acclaimed emperor, while the Senate debated restoring the Republic. He promised each praetorian 15,000 sesterces, the first emperor, as Suetonius says, to buy the soldiers' loyalty.
events.detail: Herod Agrippa I mediated between Claudius and the Senate, according to Josephus. The Senate, abandoned by the urban cohorts, yielded the next day. Claudius executed Cassius Chaerea but declared an amnesty and abolished treason trials for a time. His physical disabilities (limp, stammer, tremor) had kept him out of public life; his scholarly works on Etruscan and Carthaginian history and his proposed new letters of the alphabet reflect a learned mind. The episode showed that the praetorians could make an emperor.

events.title: Claudius's letter to the Alexandrians
events.summary: A papyrus copy (P.Lond. VI 1912), published by the prefect Lucius Aemilius Rectus on 10 November 41, preserves Claudius's reply to Alexandrian embassies: he declines a temple and high priest for himself, and orders Greeks to stop molesting Jews and Jews not to seek more privileges or bring in co-religionists from Syria and Egypt.
events.detail: Claudius threatens that if Jews persist he will proceed against them 'as fomenters of a general plague for the whole world', a phrase sometimes linked to early Christian missions, probably anachronistically. The document is one of the longest surviving texts in an emperor's own voice and shows the personal, reactive style of imperial government (Millar's 'petition and response').

sources.w: Greek Papyri in the British Museum

scholarship: Millar, The Emperor in the Roman World (1977)

events.title: Revolt of Scribonianus in Dalmatia
events.summary: Lucius Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus, legate of Dalmatia, wrote to Claudius ordering him to abdicate; within five days his two legions, VII and XI, deserted him when their eagles could not be decorated or pulled from the ground, and he was killed.
events.detail: Suetonius says Claudius was ready to comply. The loyal legions were rewarded with the titles Claudia Pia Fidelis. Among those condemned was Caecina Paetus; his wife Arria stabbed herself first and handed him the dagger with the words 'Paete, non dolet' ('It does not hurt, Paetus'). The revolt hardened Claudius's suspicion of senators and his dependence on freedmen.

events.title: Claudius begins the harbour of Portus
events.summary: To secure Rome's grain supply, Claudius began an artificial harbour two miles north of Ostia, with two curving moles and a lighthouse built on the sunken hull of the giant ship that had brought Caligula's Vatican obelisk from Egypt.
events.detail: Canals linked the harbour to the Tiber, relieving Rome from floods as well, as an inscription of 46 records (ILS 207). The basin, about 200 hectares, proved too exposed: 200 ships sank inside it in a storm in 62. Nero completed it, celebrated on sestertii with the legend PORT(us) OST(iensis) AVGVSTI. Trajan added the hexagonal inner basin c. 110-112.

events.title: Claudian invasion of Britain
events.summary: Aulus Plautius led four legions and auxiliaries across the Channel to Britain, ostensibly to restore the exiled Atrebatic king Verica. After a mutiny of troops reluctant to cross the Ocean, the army sailed in three divisions and landed unopposed.
events.detail: The imperial freedman Narcissus, sent to address the mutineers, was greeted with cries of 'Io Saturnalia!' (a joke on a slave giving orders), which shamed the soldiers into embarking. The legions were II Augusta, IX Hispana, XIV Gemina and XX; auxiliaries brought the total to perhaps 40,000. Claudius needed military prestige after his irregular accession; Britain also offered metals and a Druidic threat to suppress. A century after Caesar's raids, southern Britain was already economically tied to Gaul.
events.debate: Landing place: Richborough (fortified bridgehead ditches of 43 excavated) versus a landing near Fishbourne/Chichester.

events.title: Battle of the Medway
events.summary: A two-day battle at a river crossing, generally identified with the Medway, in which Plautius's army defeated the British forces of Togodumnus and Caratacus. 'Celtic' auxiliaries (probably Batavians) swam the river in full armour and maimed the chariot horses, while Vespasian and his brother Sabinus forced a crossing.
events.detail: On the second day Gnaeus Hosidius Geta, almost captured, won the battle and received triumphal ornaments though he had not been consul, a rare honour. The Britons fell back to the Thames, where Togodumnus died soon afterwards. Dio, our only source, names neither river.

battle.significance: Opened south-east Britain to Roman conquest.

events.title: Claudius in Britain; fall of Camulodunum
events.summary: Summoned by Plautius, Claudius crossed to Britain with praetorians and elephants, led the advance on the Catuvellaunian capital Camulodunum and received the submission of British kings, staying only sixteen days.
events.detail: His arch in Rome (dedicated 51/52) recorded that he received the surrender of eleven British kings 'without any loss' (CIL VI 920). He triumphed in 44, gave his son the name Britannicus, and placed a naval crown on the Palatine beside the civic crown, symbolising his conquest of the Ocean. Rome's first permanent fortress in Britain was built at Camulodunum.

events.title: Annexation of Lycia
events.summary: After civic strife in which Romans were killed, Claudius ended the freedom of the Lycian League and made Lycia a province, later joined with Pamphylia.
events.detail: The Stadiasmus Patarensis, a monumental pillar at Patara inscribed in 45/46, lists the roads built by the first governor Quintus Veranius with distances between Lycian cities, the most detailed road document of its kind. The League continued as a provincial assembly for the imperial cult.

events.title: Death of Agrippa I; Judaea returns to procurators
events.summary: Herod Agrippa I, whom Claudius had made king of all his grandfather Herod's territory in 41, collapsed during games at Caesarea after being hailed as a god and died days later. Judaea reverted to direct Roman rule under procurators, beginning with Cuspius Fadus.
events.detail: Josephus says an owl appeared to him as an omen; Acts 12.23 says he was 'eaten by worms' because he did not give glory to God. He had begun a 'third wall' to enclose Jerusalem's northern suburb, halted on the orders of the Syrian legate Marsus. His son Agrippa II, aged 17, was considered too young to succeed and later received smaller territories.

events.title: Storming of Maiden Castle
events.summary: The great Durotrigan hillfort in Dorset is traditionally identified as one of the more than twenty oppida taken by Vespasian and legio II Augusta. Mortimer Wheeler's excavations of 1934-37 found a 'war cemetery' of about 38 burials at the east gate, including a skeleton with an iron ballista bolt in its spine.
events.detail: Wheeler's vivid narrative of a Roman assault and massacre became a classic of British archaeology. Re-analysis by Niall Sharples (1991) and Rebecca Redfern (2011) has shown that the burials span a longer period and that most injuries were not Roman; only a few can be tied to Roman weapons, and there is no destruction layer. Nearby Hod Hill, with ballista bolts concentrated on one hut and a Roman fort in its corner, gives clearer evidence of a Roman attack.

sides.losses: unknown; perhaps a few dozen dead

battle.significance: Iconic, though archaeologically overstated, image of the Roman conquest of the south-west.

scholarship: Redfern, 'A re-appraisal of the evidence for violence in the Late Iron Age human remains from Maiden Castle', OJA 30 (2011)
events.debate: Whether a Roman assault and massacre occurred at all.

events.title: Annexation of Thrace
events.summary: After the murder of the client king Rhoemetalces III, reportedly by his wife, Claudius annexed the Thracian kingdom as a province under an equestrian procurator, completing Roman control of the Balkans south of the Danube.
events.detail: Thrace had been a client kingdom since Augustus, divided for a time between Rhoemetalces's heirs, with risings in 21 and 26 against levies. The annexation is dated by Eusebius's Chronicle and coins; the relevant books of Tacitus are lost. A senatorial legate governed Thrace from Trajan's time, and colonies were founded at Apri and Deultum.

events.title: Corbulo's operations against the Chauci and Frisii
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, legate of lower Germany, destroyed the Chaucian pirate fleet of the Cananefate deserter Gannascus, restored discipline, and imposed a Roman settlement on the Frisii. Claudius then ordered him to withdraw west of the Rhine.
events.detail: Corbulo is said to have exclaimed 'Happy the Roman generals of old!' and set his troops to dig a 23-mile canal between the Rhine and the Meuse (fossa Corbulonis), whose timber revetments near Leiden have been dated by dendrochronology to 50. He received triumphal ornaments. The episode marks Claudius's decision that the lower Rhine would not be crossed again.

events.title: Claudius's censorship and the Lyon Tablet speech
events.summary: As censor in 47-48, Claudius persuaded the Senate to admit leading men of Gallia Comata to senatorial office, beginning with the Aedui. His speech survives in his own words on a bronze tablet found at Lyon in 1528 and in Tacitus's rewritten version.
events.detail: The original (CIL XIII 1668 = ILS 212) is digressive and antiquarian, recalling the Etruscan origins of king Servius Tullius (whom he identifies with Mastarna) and including a self-address ('it is time, Tiberius Caesar Germanicus, to reveal to the conscript fathers where your speech is going'). Tacitus (Ann. 11.24) turns it into a concise argument that Rome's strength lay in absorbing conquered peoples. The comparison is the classic test case for Tacitus's handling of documents. The census of 48 counted 5,984,072 citizens, nearly a million more than in AD 14, reflecting Claudius's liberal grants of citizenship.
scholarship: Griffin, 'The Lyons Tablet and Tacitean Hindsight', CQ 32 (1982)

events.title: Fall of Messalina
events.summary: While Claudius was at Ostia, his wife Valeria Messalina publicly went through a marriage ceremony with the consul-designate Gaius Silius. The freedman Narcissus alerted the emperor, took temporary command of the praetorians and had Messalina killed in the Gardens of Lucullus.
events.detail: Tacitus admits the story seems incredible but insists it is attested by older writers. Modern interpretations see a coup attempt aimed at replacing Claudius with Silius as guardian of Britannicus, rather than mere recklessness. Claudius, at dinner, asked why the empress had not come. The Senate ordered her name and images removed. Her fall opened the way for Agrippina.

events.title: Claudius marries his niece Agrippina
events.summary: After the Senate, prompted by Lucius Vitellius, passed a decree legalising marriage between a man and his brother's daughter, Claudius married Agrippina the Younger, daughter of Germanicus and mother of Lucius Domitius (the future Nero).
events.detail: Agrippina became the most powerful woman of the Julio-Claudian age: she received the title Augusta in 50, sat on a tribunal to receive embassies, and had Seneca recalled from exile in Corsica (49) to tutor her son. The decree on uncle-niece marriage was so unusual that Tacitus says only one knight and one freedman followed the imperial example; it was repealed in 342.

events.title: Claudius expels Jews from Rome 'impulsore Chresto'
events.summary: Suetonius reports that Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews 'who were continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus', usually understood as conflict in the synagogues over Christian preaching about Christ. Acts 18.2 says the couple Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth because of this edict.
events.detail: Orosius dates the expulsion to 49, citing Josephus, though no such passage exists in Josephus's surviving works. Dio (60.6.6) says that in 41 Claudius did not expel the Jews but forbade them to assemble, leading some to place the measure in 41. Whether Chrestus was Christ, or a local agitator, remains debated. It is possibly the earliest pagan reference to Christianity.
events.debate: Date (41 vs 49), extent, and identity of Chrestus.

events.title: Foundation of the colony of Camulodunum
events.summary: Publius Ostorius Scapula moved legio XX west and founded Colonia Claudia Victricensis at Camulodunum, the first chartered Roman town in Britain, as a veteran settlement and model of urban life, with a temple to the deified Claudius.
events.detail: Tacitus calls the temple 'a citadel of eternal domination' in British eyes, its priests 'pouring out whole fortunes under the pretext of religion'. The veterans' seizure of Trinovantian land was a main cause of the Boudican revolt. The podium of the temple survives beneath the Norman castle of Colchester.

events.title: Claudius adopts Nero
events.summary: Under Agrippina's influence Claudius adopted her son Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, who became Nero Claudius Caesar Drusus Germanicus, giving him precedence over Claudius's own younger son Britannicus.
events.detail: Nero assumed the toga virilis early, in 51, was designated consul for his twentieth year, received proconsular imperium outside Rome and the title princeps iuventutis, and married Claudius's daughter Octavia in 53. Agrippina gradually removed Britannicus's supporters, including his tutors and the praetorian prefects, replaced by her ally Afranius Burrus as sole prefect (51).

events.title: Caratacus's last battle
events.summary: Publius Ostorius Scapula stormed the hill position, defended by a stone rampart above a river, where Caratacus had made his stand among the Ordovices. Caratacus's wife, daughter and brothers were captured; he fled to Cartimandua of the Brigantes, who handed him over in chains.
events.detail: Brought to Rome, Caratacus addressed Claudius and Agrippina so nobly (in Tacitus's version) that they pardoned him and his family; Dio has him remark, on seeing the city, 'Why do you, who have all this, covet our poor tents?' Tacitus compares his capture to those of Syphax and Perseus. The Silures fought on, defeating a legion under Manlius Valens, and Ostorius died worn out in 52.
events.locName: Hill site in Ordovician territory (Cefn Carnedd? Llanymynech?)

sides.strength: Legions with auxiliaries (XIV and XX likely)

battle.significance: Ended the resistance of Caratacus, the most famous British leader before Boudica.

events.title: Claudius's letter naming Gallio proconsul of Achaea
events.summary: A fragmentary letter of Claudius inscribed at Delphi, dated after his 26th imperatorial acclamation (52), names Lucius Junius Gallio, Seneca's brother, as proconsul of Achaea. Since Acts 18.12-17 says Paul was brought before Gallio at Corinth, the inscription is the single fixed point in Pauline chronology.
events.detail: Gallio's proconsulship is usually placed in 51/52, putting Paul's eighteen-month stay in Corinth about 50-52. The letter itself concerns the depopulation of Delphi and invites new citizens to settle there. Gallio later fell victim to Nero after the Pisonian conspiracy.

events.title: Opening of the Fucine Lake emissary
events.summary: After eleven years' work by 30,000 men, Claudius inaugurated a 5.6 km tunnel to drain the Fucine Lake into the Liris, staging first a naumachia with 19,000 condemned combatants, whose greeting 'Hail emperor, those about to die salute you' is reported by Suetonius.
events.detail: The first opening failed because the channel was too shallow; at the second, the rush of water nearly swept away the banqueting stand, and Agrippina blamed Narcissus for profiteering. The tunnel silted up after Claudius's death; Trajan and Hadrian repaired it, and the lake was finally drained by Prince Alessandro Torlonia in 1875-78.

events.title: Death of Claudius
events.summary: Claudius died aged 63, almost certainly poisoned by Agrippina with a dish of mushrooms prepared by the poisoner Locusta and served by the taster Halotus; when he vomited, the doctor Xenophon finished him with a poisoned feather.
events.detail: The death was concealed until Nero could be presented to the praetorians at noon. Claudius was deified, but Seneca's satire Apocolocyntosis ('Pumpkinification') mocked his admission to heaven, and Nero later joked that mushrooms were the food of the gods. Modern scholars accept poisoning as likely, though natural death has advocates.

events.title: Accession of Nero
events.summary: The 16-year-old Nero was presented by the prefect Burrus to the praetorians, who hailed him emperor; the Senate followed. His first speech, written by Seneca, promised to end secret trials in the palace and the power of freedmen and to restore the Senate's functions.
events.detail: The early years (the 'quinquennium Neronis', which Trajan reportedly called the best period of any emperor, according to Aurelius Victor) were managed by Seneca and Burrus. Seneca's De clementia, addressed to Nero in 55-56, sets out an ideal of monarchy restrained by mercy. Agrippina's influence, initially paramount (coins show her facing Nero), was soon curtailed.
events.debate: Whether the 'quinquennium' refers to the first five years of the reign or to a later period, and whether Trajan's remark concerned building rather than government.

events.title: Murder of Britannicus
events.summary: Claudius's son Britannicus, approaching his fourteenth birthday, collapsed at a family dinner after drinking a hot drink cooled with poisoned water, the taster having tested only the hot drink. Nero said it was an epileptic fit; he was buried that night.
events.detail: The poison was again supplied by Locusta. Agrippina, who had threatened to champion Britannicus against her son, and Octavia, Britannicus's sister, had to conceal their horror. Tacitus says Nero had earlier made the boy sing at a Saturnalia party, and he sang of his lost inheritance.

events.title: Corbulo takes Artaxata
events.summary: Advancing in three columns after storming the fortress of Volandum, Corbulo forced Tiridates to abandon Artaxata, the Armenian capital, which opened its gates; the inhabitants were spared but the city was razed because it could not be garrisoned.
events.detail: Tacitus records that a sudden brilliant light falling on the city was taken as a sign that the gods wished it destroyed. Nero was hailed imperator and the Senate voted extravagant honours. Corbulo then marched to Tigranocerta (59), which surrendered. Artaxata was later rebuilt by Tiridates as Neroneia.

sides.strength: Legions III Gallica and VI Ferrata with auxiliaries and allies

battle.significance: Drove the Parthian-backed king out of his capital.

events.title: Murder of Agrippina the Younger
events.summary: During the Quinquatria festival at Baiae, Nero tried to drown his mother in a collapsible boat designed by Anicetus, prefect of the Misenum fleet. She swam ashore; Nero then sent Anicetus with marines to kill her at her villa, where she bade them strike her womb.
events.detail: Nero claimed she had plotted against him and committed suicide when exposed; Seneca drafted the letter to the Senate, and Burrus refused to use the praetorians against Germanicus's daughter. The Senate voted thanksgivings. Tacitus's account (Ann. 14.1-13) is among his most celebrated narratives. Dio, Suetonius and the play Octavia offer variants. Agrippina's memoirs, now lost, were used by Tacitus and Pliny.

events.title: Riot in the amphitheatre at Pompeii
events.summary: At gladiatorial games given by the expelled senator Livineius Regulus, abuse between Pompeians and visitors from neighbouring Nuceria escalated into a riot in which many Nucerians were killed or wounded. The Senate banned games at Pompeii for ten years and dissolved illegal associations.
events.detail: A fresco from a house in Pompeii (I.3.23), now in Naples, shows the fighting in and around the amphitheatre, with the awning (velarium) and stalls outside, one of the very few contemporary images of a historical event from a provincial town. Graffiti mocking Nucerians have also been found.

events.title: Nero's expedition to the sources of the Nile
events.summary: Around 61-63 Nero sent a party of praetorians under two centurions south through Meroë; Seneca says they reached immense marshes so choked with vegetation that only a single-man boat could pass, probably the Sudd of South Sudan.
events.detail: Seneca heard the report from the centurions themselves; Pliny the Elder gives their measured distances from Syene to Meroë (871 miles) and observations on the decline of Meroë. The mission may have been reconnaissance for a planned Ethiopian war. It was the furthest documented Roman penetration into sub-Saharan Africa along the Nile.

events.title: Plautius Silvanus resettles 100,000 Transdanubians
events.summary: Tiberius Plautius Silvanus Aelianus, legate of Moesia under Nero, brought more than 100,000 people from across the Danube, with wives, children and chiefs, into the province as tribute-payers, checked a Sarmatian movement, relieved the siege of Chersonesus in the Crimea and sent grain to Rome.
events.detail: These achievements are known only from his funerary elogium near Tibur (ILS 986), which also records that Vespasian granted him the triumphal ornaments that Nero had withheld. It is the earliest documented case of mass settlement of barbarians inside the empire, a practice that became routine under Marcus Aurelius and later emperors.

events.title: Suetonius Paullinus's assault on Mona
events.summary: Suetonius Paullinus crossed the Menai Strait with infantry in flat-bottomed boats and cavalry fording or swimming, to attack Mona (Anglesey), refuge of fugitives and centre of Druidism. The soldiers, frozen by the sight of women in black with torches and Druids pouring curses, were urged on and slaughtered the defenders.
events.detail: The sacred groves, where Tacitus says altars were drenched with captives' blood, were cut down. As a garrison was being installed, news arrived of Boudica's revolt. Agricola, then a young tribune on Paullinus's staff, retook the island in 77/78.

sides.strength: Legio XIV, part of XX and auxiliaries

battle.significance: Struck at the Druidic centre but left the province exposed to Boudica.

events.title: Boudica sacks Camulodunum
events.summary: On the death of Prasutagus, whose will named Nero co-heir with his daughters, Roman officials seized the Icenian kingdom, flogged his widow Boudica and raped their daughters. The Iceni and Trinovantes rose and stormed the unwalled colony of Camulodunum, whose last defenders held the Temple of Claudius for two days.
events.detail: Legio IX Hispana under Petillius Cerialis, marching to the rescue, lost its infantry; Cerialis escaped with the cavalry. The procurator Catus Decianus fled to Gaul. A thick burnt layer of 60/61 runs through Colchester, and a bronze head of Claudius found in the River Alde in Suffolk may be loot from the colony. Omens included the fall of the statue of Victory with its back turned 'as though fleeing the enemy'.

sides.strength: Iceni and Trinovantes in great numbers
Veterans, 200 men sent by the procurator; relieving force of legio IX
sides.losses: colony destroyed; IX Hispana's infantry (perhaps 2,000) killed

battle.significance: The worst Roman disaster in Britain, opening the road to Londinium.

events.title: Destruction of Londinium and Verulamium
events.summary: Suetonius Paullinus reached Londinium, already a busy trading town, but judged it indefensible and abandoned it; the rebels destroyed it and the municipium of Verulamium. Tacitus says 70,000 citizens and allies died in the three towns, killed by gibbet, fire and cross.
events.detail: A red burnt horizon of the period is found across the early City of London. Dio describes atrocities against noblewomen in a grove of the goddess Andraste. The procurator who replaced Catus, Julius Classicianus, whose tombstone survives in the British Museum, later reported that reprisals were prolonging the war.

events.title: Defeat of Boudica
events.summary: Suetonius Paullinus, with legio XIV, detachments of XX and auxiliaries, almost 10,000 men, chose a defile with a forest behind and open plain before. The British host, with families watching from wagons, charged and was broken by javelin volleys and a wedge attack; the wagons blocked their flight.
events.detail: Tacitus reports nearly 80,000 Britons and 400 Romans killed, figures no one accepts at face value; Dio gives the Britons 230,000. Boudica poisoned herself (Tacitus) or died of illness (Dio). Poenius Postumus, camp prefect of legio II Augusta, who had refused orders to join, fell on his sword. Famine followed because the Britons had not sown crops. Nero's freedman Polyclitus was sent to investigate, and Paullinus was soon replaced by the conciliatory Petronius Turpilianus.

battle.significance: Saved the province of Britain for Rome.

events.debate: Site (Mancetter, High Cross, Church Stowe, near Towcester and others) and year (60 or 61).

events.title: Murder of Pedanius Secundus and execution of his 400 slaves
events.summary: The city prefect Lucius Pedanius Secundus was murdered by one of his slaves. Under the senatus consultum Silanianum all slaves under the same roof were liable to execution; despite popular riots and some senatorial opposition, all 400 were put to death.
events.detail: Tacitus gives the jurist Gaius Cassius Longinus a speech insisting that only fear could control households 'containing nations of slaves with foreign rites or none'. Soldiers lined the route to prevent the crowd rescuing the condemned. A proposal to deport Pedanius's freedmen too was vetoed by Nero. The episode is a key text for Roman slavery and its legal violence.

events.title: Death of Burrus, retirement of Seneca and murder of Octavia
events.summary: In 62 the praetorian prefect Burrus died (perhaps poisoned), Seneca asked leave to retire and offered back his fortune, and Nero divorced Octavia on a charge of sterility, exiled her to Pandateria on a trumped-up charge of adultery and had her killed, to marry Poppaea Sabina.
events.detail: Burrus was replaced by Ofonius Tigellinus and Faenius Rufus. The same year the treason law was revived for the praetor Antistius Sosianus, who had recited satirical verses about Nero (Thrasea Paetus secured a lesser penalty), and the exiled Rubellius Plautus and Faustus Cornelius Sulla were murdered. Octavia's head was brought to Poppaea. The pseudo-Senecan tragedy Octavia dramatises her fate. Tacitus marks 62 as the decisive turn of the reign.

events.title: Capitulation of Paetus at Rhandeia
events.summary: Lucius Caesennius Paetus, sent to annex Armenia outright, dispersed his forces and was besieged by Vologases at Rhandeia on the Arsanias. With Corbulo's relief army three days away, he capitulated, agreeing to evacuate Armenia and to build a bridge over the river for the Parthians.
events.detail: Rumour said the legions IV Scythica and XII Fulminata passed under the yoke. Paetus had earlier sent Nero dispatches announcing victory. Nero pardoned him with a joke that a man so prone to panic might fall ill from prolonged suspense. In Rome trophies for victory were already standing on the Capitol. The defeat led to the Rhandeia compromise of 63, negotiated on the same spot by Corbulo.
events.locName: Rhandeia on the Arsanias (Murat), near Harput

sides.strength: Legions IV Scythica and XII Fulminata (understrength) with auxiliaries

battle.significance: Forced Rome to accept an Arsacid king of Armenia.

events.title: Earthquake in Campania
events.summary: A severe earthquake damaged Pompeii, Herculaneum and Nuceria on 5 February. Seneca says a flock of 600 sheep died, statues split, and people went mad. Many buildings in Pompeii were still under repair when Vesuvius erupted seventeen years later.
events.detail: A marble relief from the lararium of the banker Lucius Caecilius Iucundus at Pompeii shows the temple of Jupiter and the Vesuvius gate tilting in the quake. Seneca's Natural Questions (book 6) was prompted by it and dates it to 63; Tacitus places it in 62.

events.title: Annexation of Pontus Polemoniacus
events.summary: With the consent of its king Polemon II, Nero annexed the Pontic kingdom on the Black Sea coast to the province of Galatia-Cappadocia; the Cottian Alps became a procuratorial province around the same time on the death of Cottius II.
events.detail: Trapezus became the base of the Pontic fleet (classis Pontica), whose control of the eastern Black Sea was important in the Armenian wars. Polemon received compensation in Cilicia. The annexation continued the Julio-Claudian policy of absorbing client kingdoms when convenient.

events.title: Great Fire of Rome
events.summary: Fire broke out in the shops by the Circus Maximus on the night of 18/19 July and burned for six days, then flared again from Tigellinus's estates for three more. Of Rome's fourteen regions three were destroyed, seven badly damaged and four untouched.
events.detail: Nero, at Antium, returned to organise relief, opened the Campus Martius, Agrippa's buildings and his own gardens to the homeless, and cut the price of grain to 3 sesterces. Rumour that he had sung of the fall of Troy while Rome burned (on a private stage, Tacitus says; from the tower of Maecenas, Suetonius) and that he started the fire to rebuild the city in his name was never dispelled. His new building code required wider streets, limited heights, porticoes, fireproof Gabine or Alban stone in party walls and accessible water. Tacitus noted the fire began on the same day as the Gallic sack of 390 BC.
events.debate: Responsibility: accident, Nero, or (as Nero alleged) Christians; Tacitus himself leaves it open.

events.title: Nero's punishment of the Christians
events.summary: To deflect blame for the fire, Nero punished 'those whom the crowd called Christians, hated for their abominations'. A huge number were convicted 'not so much of arson as of hatred of the human race', torn by dogs in animal skins, crucified, or burned as torches at night in Nero's gardens.
events.detail: Tacitus's account (Ann. 15.44) is the earliest pagan description of Christians as a group; he notes that the cruelty eventually provoked pity. Suetonius lists the punishment of Christians, 'a new and mischievous superstition', among Nero's police measures, without linking it to the fire. Christian tradition (1 Clement 5-6, Eusebius) places the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul in Rome under Nero. Brent Shaw (2015) argued that Tacitus retrojected a later situation and that no Neronian persecution of 'Christians' as such occurred; most scholars still accept a Neronian action against the group.
scholarship: Shaw, 'The Myth of the Neronian Persecution', JRS 105 (2015)
Jones, 'The historicity of the Neronian persecution', NTS 63 (2017)
events.debate: Historicity and scope of the persecution.

events.title: Nero's Golden House
events.summary: On land cleared by the fire Nero built the Domus Aurea, a palace-landscape stretching from the Palatine to the Esquiline, with a colossal bronze statue of himself 120 feet high, an artificial lake, vineyards and woods. On moving in he said he could at last live like a human being.
events.detail: The architects Severus and Celer built vaulted halls including the octagonal room on the Oppian hill, an early masterpiece of concrete architecture; Suetonius describes a main dining room that rotated day and night like the heavens. Its wall paintings, by Famulus, were rediscovered around 1480 by artists who lowered themselves into the buried rooms (the 'grottoes'), inspiring Raphael's grotesques. The Flavians gave the site back to the public: the Colosseum rose over the lake and Trajan's baths over the Oppian wing.

events.title: Nero's coinage reform
events.summary: Around 64 Nero reduced the aureus from 1/40 to 1/45 of a Roman pound and the denarius from 1/84 to 1/96, while lowering the silver fineness of the denarius from about 97-98% to about 93%. Base-metal coinage was also reorganised, with brass asses briefly struck.
events.detail: The reform may have been prompted by the cost of rebuilding after the fire, by shortages of bullion, or by a desire to align the gold-silver ratio; the reduced standards lasted until Trajan's further debasement. Pliny notes the reduction of the aureus. Neronian sestertii of the period are among the finest Roman coin dies.
scholarship: Butcher and Ponting, The Metallurgy of Roman Silver Coinage (2014)
MacDowall, The Western Coinages of Nero (1979)

events.title: Pisonian conspiracy
events.summary: A broad conspiracy of senators, equites and praetorian officers planned to kill Nero at the Circus games of the Cerialia and make the aristocrat Gaius Calpurnius Piso emperor. It was betrayed the day before by Milichus, freedman of the conspirator Flavius Scaevinus.
events.detail: Nineteen were killed and thirteen exiled. The freedwoman Epicharis endured torture without naming anyone and strangled herself with her breast-band. The praetorian prefect Faenius Rufus, himself a conspirator, conducted interrogations until exposed. The tribune Subrius Flavus told Nero he hated him as a matricide, charioteer, actor and arsonist. Seneca was ordered to die and opened his veins in a slow, philosophical death; the poet Lucan recited his own verses as he bled. Petronius and Thrasea Paetus followed in 66 in the aftermath.

events.title: Coronation of Tiridates in Rome
events.summary: Under the Rhandeia settlement, the Arsacid Tiridates travelled overland to Rome (avoiding the sea for religious reasons as a Zoroastrian magus) with 3,000 Parthian horsemen and received the diadem from Nero in the Forum, kneeling as to Mithras; the doors of Janus were closed.
events.detail: The nine-month journey cost the treasury 800,000 sesterces a day. The ceremony, staged at dawn with the Forum packed and the praetorians in arms, was followed by a gilded day at the theatre of Pompey (the 'Golden Day'). Pliny the Elder says Tiridates initiated Nero into magic banquets. The settlement kept peace on the eastern frontier until Trajan.

events.title: Outbreak of the Jewish revolt
events.summary: After the procurator Gessius Florus seized 17 talents from the Temple treasury and let his troops massacre Jerusalemites, the Temple captain Eleazar son of Ananias stopped the daily sacrifices for the emperor, effectively declaring revolt. Rebels took the Antonia fortress and Masada, and the Roman garrison was massacred after surrendering.
events.detail: Agrippa II's speech urging submission (BJ 2.345-404), with its survey of the Roman army's deployment across the empire, is a Josephan composition but a valuable statement of Roman power. Violence spread to mixed cities: Caesarea's Jews were massacred, and Jews and Greeks fought in Scythopolis, Alexandria and Syria. The Sicarii leader Menahem, who had armed his men from Herod's arsenal at Masada, was killed by rival rebels. Moderate aristocrats under the former high priest Ananus took charge of the government.

events.title: Defeat of Cestius Gallus at Beth Horon
events.summary: Cestius Gallus, legate of Syria, marched on Jerusalem with legio XII Fulminata, vexillations of other legions and allied troops, assaulted the Temple, then inexplicably withdrew. In the pass of Beth Horon his column was ambushed and routed, abandoning its baggage and artillery.
events.detail: Josephus gives Roman losses of 5,300 infantry and 480 cavalry; Suetonius says an eagle was lost. The rebels used the captured artillery in the defence of Jerusalem in 70. The victory convinced many waverers that God was with the revolt and led to the organisation of a rebel government with regional commanders, Josephus among them in Galilee. Nero then appointed Vespasian.

sides.strength: Legio XII Fulminata, 2,000 from each of three other legions, 6 cohorts, 4 alae and allied troops: c. 30,000

battle.significance: Turned a riot into a full-scale war and brought Vespasian to Judaea.

events.title: Nero's tour of Greece and the liberation of Achaea
events.summary: During a tour of Greece in 66-67, Nero competed in all the great games, which were rescheduled into a single year, and won 1,808 crowns. At the Isthmian Games on 28 November 67 he proclaimed the freedom of Achaea from Roman taxation and governors, and he cut the first sod of a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth.
events.detail: His speech survives on an inscription from Acraephia in Boeotia (ILS 8794), deliberately echoing Flamininus's proclamation of Greek freedom in 196 BC. At Olympia he fell from a ten-horse chariot but was crowned anyway. The canal was dug by soldiers and 6,000 Jewish prisoners sent by Vespasian, but abandoned after his death; the modern canal (1881-1893) follows its line. Vespasian revoked Greek freedom.

events.title: Forced suicide of Corbulo
events.summary: Summoned to Greece by Nero with flattering letters, the greatest general of the age was met at Cenchreae with an order to die; he stabbed himself saying 'Axios', 'I deserved it', meaning he had been a fool to trust Nero. The Scribonii brothers, commanders in Germany, died at the same time.
events.detail: Corbulo's son-in-law Annius Vinicianus had been implicated in a conspiracy at Beneventum in 66. The removal of the most prestigious commanders left the armies without loyalty to Nero, a factor in his fall a year later. Corbulo's daughter Domitia Longina married Domitian.

events.title: Siege of Jotapata
events.summary: Vespasian besieged the Galilean hill town of Jotapata, defended by Josephus, for 47 days, with earth ramps, rams and 160 artillery engines. The town fell at dawn after a deserter revealed the exhausted sentries slept; Josephus hid in a cave with forty others who agreed on a suicide pact by lot, and survived to surrender.
events.detail: Josephus says 40,000 died (a figure inflated) and 1,200 were captured. His description of defensive devices (boiling oil, fenugreek poured on boarding planks, sacks to deaden ram blows) is vivid and self-serving. Brought before Vespasian, he predicted that Vespasian and Titus would become emperors; when this was fulfilled in 69 he was freed and took the name Flavius. The 'Josephus problem' in mathematics derives from his survival of the lots.

sides.strength: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XV Apollinaris with auxiliaries
sides.losses: light; Vespasian wounded in the foot

battle.significance: Broke organised resistance in Galilee and delivered Josephus, the war's historian, into Roman hands.

scholarship: Aviam, 'Yodefat-Jotapata: the archaeology of the first battle', in Berlin and Overman (eds), The First Jewish Revolt (2002)

events.title: Siege of Gamla
events.summary: Gamla, perched on a camel-hump ridge in the Golan, repulsed Vespasian's first assault when Roman troops who broke in were trapped in collapsing houses. A month later, after a tower was undermined, Titus stormed it; Josephus says 4,000 were killed and 5,000 threw themselves into the ravine, only two women surviving.
events.detail: Excavations since 1976 (Gutman, Syon) have revealed the breach in the wall, some 1,600 iron arrowheads, 2,000 ballista stones, and one of the oldest known synagogues, as well as coins struck by the rebels 'for the redemption of Jerusalem the holy'. Gamla is one of the best-preserved Roman siege sites anywhere.
scholarship: Syon, Gamla III: The Shmarya Gutmann Excavations (2014)

events.title: Revolt of Vindex
events.summary: Gaius Julius Vindex, an Aquitanian noble descended from kings and governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, rose against Nero in March 68, calling on the provincial governors to free the world from a tyrant who sang on the stage, and offered the throne to Galba in Spain.
events.detail: Vindex had no legions but raised large Gallic levies (Plutarch says 100,000). His coins bore no emperor's portrait, with slogans such as SALVS GENERIS HVMANI and SIGNA P(opuli) R(omani). Nero reportedly cared most that Vindex had called him a bad lyre-player. Whether Vindex sought Gallic independence (as later Roman writers implied) or simply the overthrow of Nero is debated; most modern historians favour the latter.

events.title: Battle of Vesontio
events.summary: Lucius Verginius Rufus, commanding upper Germany, marched against Vindex, who was besieging Vesontio. After the two leaders apparently came to terms, their armies clashed anyway and the Rhine legions slaughtered some 20,000 Gauls; Vindex killed himself.
events.detail: The legions then offered Verginius the throne, which he refused, declaring that the Senate and people should choose. His epitaph, which he composed himself and Pliny quotes, claimed he had 'claimed the empire not for himself but for his country'. The battle showed that the Rhine armies, not Gallic levies, held the balance of power.

battle.significance: Destroyed Vindex but left Nero without the loyalty of the Rhine legions.

events.title: Galba proclaimed at Carthago Nova
events.summary: Servius Sulpicius Galba, the 71-year-old governor of Hispania Tarraconensis, of ancient nobility, declared himself legate of the Senate and Roman people at Carthago Nova, raising a new legion (VII Galbiana) from provincials. Otho, governor of Lusitania, joined him.
events.detail: Declared a public enemy by the Senate, he despaired after Vindex's defeat until news came that Nero was dead and he had been recognised. In Africa the legate Clodius Macer also revolted, cutting off grain to Rome and raising a legion (I Macriana), and was later killed on Galba's orders.

events.title: Death of Nero
events.summary: Deserted by the praetorians, whose prefect Nymphidius Sabinus had promised them a vast donative in Galba's name, and declared a public enemy by the Senate, Nero fled to the villa of his freedman Phaon four miles from Rome and stabbed himself with the help of his secretary Epaphroditus, saying 'What an artist dies with me!'
events.detail: He was 30. His nurses and his former mistress Acte buried him in the family tomb of the Domitii on the Pincian. With him the Julio-Claudian dynasty ended. Popular affection, especially in the Greek East, produced 'false Neros' in 69, around 80 and in 88, and Christian apocalyptic belief in Nero redivivus (echoed in Revelation). Suetonius says flowers were laid on his tomb for years.
events.locName: Villa of Phaon, between the Via Salaria and Via Nomentana
